_note: Where a run happens. A map changes all four of the things the owner asked for: the ground and its tileset, the node and enemy mix, the arena's size and shape, and the hazards standing on it. Everything here is content — adding a sixth map is this file plus nothing.
_rngNote: THE MAP IS THE FIRST DRAW OFF THE RUN'S SEEDED RNG. World's constructor picks it immediately after `new Rng(seed)` and before anything else touches the stream. That position is load-bearing and must not move: insert the choice anywhere later and every draw after it shifts, so every existing seed replays as a different run. It is first rather than last because it is the only decision the whole rest of the run is conditioned on — arena size feeds the spatial grid, which is built before the field is scattered.
_areaConfoundNote: Arena AREA is held near the Home Field's 3.84M on every map except the Scrapyard, which is small on purpose. Shape is the feature; area is a confound. The first pass varied both, and the two largest maps (theBurn at 4.75M, boneOrchard at 4.32M) measurably inverted The Kid's class identity in run.test.ts — a class whose damage scales with velocity needs enemies to run PAST, and on a big enough field a kiting bot just runs into empty ground and deals nothing. Holding area roughly constant keeps five genuinely different shapes without turning arena size into a stealth difficulty knob.
_shapeNote: 'Shape' here means the rectangle's proportions, not a non-rectangular arena. A 3200x1200 flat and a 1600x2600 corridor play very differently — sightlines, how far a kite can run before a wall, how much of the field the camera holds — and they cost nothing in the collision or clamping code, which stays a rectangle. A genuinely non-rectangular arena would touch the spatial grid, the edge spawner and the player clamp; it is not what this is.
_areaNote: Node counts are per-map rather than scaled from area, because density is the design lever and area is only one input to it. The Scrapyard is the smallest arena AND the sparsest field: cramped and stripped, nowhere to run and little to harvest. The Bone Orchard is the largest AND the densest, which is what makes it the map you go to for feed.
_densityNote: HOW MANY are standing at once is `life / everySeconds`, NOT `maxLive`. The first pass set maxLive to 9-14 and everySeconds to 5-13 and got one to three live hazards, because one spawn per interval that lives `life` seconds settles at that ratio long before it reaches any cap. maxLive is a safety cap, not a target. Every map below now sets `everySeconds` to about `life / (intended live count)` so the two numbers agree, and maxLive sits a little above the equilibrium to absorb the jitter. Change `life` and you have changed the density — come back and change `everySeconds` with it.
_groundStockNote: Nineteen unwired Wang sets -- the session 17 ten (soil_to_pasture, pasture_to_{hardpan,bog,ashfall,scree,saltcrust}, earth_to_pasture_plain, pasture_to_{withered,rot,ash}_plain) plus nine later alternates of already-wired transitions -- were RETIRED in the scene-pass audit rather than wired blind. Session 17's own finding is why: the first family was generated at 'highly detailed' with decorative nouns and at 32px that becomes a REPEATING MOTIF -- the pasture read as polka dots, the hardpan as red brickwork, enemies invisible against it -- and even the better second family 'still carries a faint repeat that dirt_to_grass_plain does not'. That is a combat-readability call that needs a human watching two hundred enemies move across it, which this pass could not do, so the files were deleted from `assets/tilesets/` rather than left as a permanent packed-unused line nobody owns. RULE FOR NEXT TIME: for ground, ask for less -- and playtest before wiring, not after.
_hazardNote: Ambient hazards belong to the map, not the wave. They damage ENEMIES as well as the player (`dps` and `playerDps` are separate), so a burning patch is a tool as much as a tax — the fight becomes about where you stand, which is the whole reason a map should own hazards. The Home Field has none on purpose: it is the baseline the game has always played as, and it stays exactly that.

homeField.name: The Home Field
homeField.blurb: Your own ground, going wrong on schedule.

place._note: The Home Field as a place (src/render/place.ts). The arena is the fenced field; the farmstead stands outside it to the north, corn runs down both sides, and the crop duster lies where it came down, south of the road. The camera may look margin px past the fence. Nothing out there collides: nothing in the fight can reach it.

ground._grassNote: Flat tones, on purpose (critic rounds 3-4, 'blotchy camouflage'). grass_to_soil and lush_overgrown_to_cold_grey carry a speckle pattern every few pixels; the shader's own tufts, flowers and stepped light give the texture, and three busy tiles under them read as camo.
ground._blightNote: Picked off a contact sheet of every wang tile (critic round 2). grass_to_rot and grass_to_greybrown both carry hard horizontal bands that repeat every tile, and under a sundown grade they read as rust-coloured static across the whole field. These three are organic mottles: dry gold, dead beige-grey, grey-green ash.

place._tilledNote: Four worked fields, one to a quadrant, with grass headlands between them and the lanes: the run happens ON the field the title sells. Until critic round 8 there were three small plots and the rest was lawn ('a flat olive lawn crossed by straight dirt paths'). Ground only; nothing here is read by the sim.

saltFlats.name: The Salt Flats
saltFlats.blurb: Nothing grows and nothing hides. Neither do you.
saltFlats._biasNote: Open ground with long sightlines rewards speed and punishes anything that lumbers. The fast roster gets commoner and the two slowest heavies get rarer — a maskedHauler crossing 3200px of flat is a slow-motion telegraph rather than a threat.
saltFlats._tuningNote: First pass was a 3200x1200 flat with rooster and duckFlight at 1.8, which measured 40% cleared against the Home Field's 55% over 60 headless runs. Two compounding costs: the longest walk in the game between anything worth killing, and a roster stripped of the slow things a kiting bot farms. Pulled in to 2900x1300 and the multipliers toward 1. Still the widest arena and still the fast map.

hazards._note: Salt pans vent. Small, frequent, short-lived, and they expand — you get pushed off ground rather than denied it outright.

place._note: The Salt Flats as a place: the Whitacres' back forty, where the spray settled into the low ground and dried to a crust. Pale, open and nearly empty on purpose. A barbed-wire line rings it; out past the wire there is a dead windmill over a dry stock pond, a wagon somebody walked away from, bones, and a county road along the south with the posts of an older fence beside it. Nothing grows and nothing hides.

scrapyard.name: The Scrapyard
scrapyard.blurb: Square, close, and full of things that were machines.
scrapyard._biasNote: The smallest arena in the game, so the roster goes heavy. There is nowhere to kite a maskedHauler to, which is the point — this is the map where you have to kill the thing in front of you. Fliers get rare because a lane needs somewhere to go.

hazards._note: Oil sumps. Big, long-lived, and they slow rather than burn — the damage is that you are still standing there when the next group arrives.

place._note: The Scrapyard as a place: the Whitacre machine yard, where equipment went when it stopped. A board fence around a gravel lot; out past it every side is crowded with what used to be machines: the combine that seized in '79, tractors, a burnt-out combine still smoking from this morning, drums of the spray stacked where the duster crew left them, and scrap in heaps. The dark pools are oil.

theBurn.name: The Burn
theBurn.blurb: A tall strip of field somebody already set fire to.
theBurn._biasNote: Burnt ground grows the things that thrive on rot. The acid and spray roster gets commoner, and plain farmhand chaff gets rarer — this map is about hazards you can be pushed into, so the enemies that push are the ones worth having.
theBurn._tuningNote: First pass was acidZombie 2.0 / bloatedFarmhand 1.8 / maskedSprayer 1.6 / farmhand 0.7 in a 1600x2600 arena, which measured 21% cleared against the Home Field's 32% over the headless bot — the only map in the set below baseline. Stripping the cheap chaff out of the roster and replacing it with 40hp acid in the narrowest arena in the game compounded: nothing to kill quickly, nowhere to go. Widened to 1900 and the multipliers pulled toward 1. This wants a human playtest, not more bot passes; see NOTES.md.

hazards._note: Live fire. Small, hot and it hurts enemies more than it hurts you — the tall arena means you are usually able to choose which side of one to be on.

place._note: The Burn as a place: the long south strip, burnt off this morning to stop whatever the spray started, and it did not stop it. A charred rail fence, a ploughed fire break down both sides, the tenant house scorched to the frame, the combine that caught and is still smoking, and burn barrels nobody has put out. West of the break the wheat stands; east of it the fire jumped and the corn is black stalks.

boneOrchard.name: The Bone Orchard
boneOrchard.blurb: The biggest field, the best harvest, and it is a graveyard.
boneOrchard._biasNote: Bone meal makes things grow, which is why this is the feed map. What it grows is the shambling half of the roster — nothing fast, everything that used to be a person.
boneOrchard._tuningNote: First pass was a 2600x1900 field with the fast half of the roster cut to 0.6-0.7, which measured 29% cleared against the Home Field's 55% over 60 headless runs — the worst map in the set. The biggest arena and the slowest enemies is a bad pair: the field never comes to you, so the run under-levels and arrives at wave 20 three tiers short. Pulled in to 2400x1800 and the multipliers toward 1.

hazards._note: Grave damp. Rare, wide and slow — barely lethal on its own, but it sits on the ground you wanted to harvest.

place._note: The Bone Orchard as a place: the old orchard on the rise where the Whitacres have always buried their own. The family plot stands north of the fence behind a white picket, three rows deep, and the front row was dug today. Apple rows run down both sides and across the road to the south, a few of them already rotting on the branch. The grass is the greenest on the farm.

maps._previewNote: theVault below is a preview map, not part of the run rotation. It exists so `npm run shot` can render the base's floor and props before the level system is built. It carries weight 0 -- `pickMapId` never selects it -- so it changes no seed and no test.

theBottoms.name: The Bottoms
theBottoms.blurb: The low ground never drained. Whatever went into the water is still in it.
theBottoms._note: The sixth surface map, and the first built entirely from art that was already paid for: its ground, its two node variants and its hazard decal were all pulled off the account in session 25 rather than generated. It is the template for the Feedlot, the Orchard and the Dustbowl, whose ground is packed and waiting.
theBottoms._weightNote: ZERO -- built, complete, tested and NOT in the rotation. Putting it in costs exactly one seed on an acceptance bar the owner owns: with six surface maps instead of five, `tests/run.test.ts` has the Hand idle-buy bot clearing 6 of 24 standing still against a cap of 5. That number did not move when the bias was retuned hard (duckFlight 2.1 -> 1.3, the mud given real damage), which says it is not this map being soft -- it is that a sixth map reshuffles which map every seed rolls, and one seed lands better. Tuning against that is tuning against noise, and raising the cap is not on the table. So it waits for the owner: `"weight": 1` is the whole switch.

arena._note: 2700x1500 is 1.80, an aspect no other map uses, and the area is 4.05M against the Home Field's 3.84M -- close enough not to be a stealth difficulty knob. Wide and shallow on purpose: a bog you cross rather than a field you hold.

nodes._variantNote: Cattails and reeds are the whole point -- they are weight-0 crop variants in nodes.json and this is the first map to raise them. Wet ground grows reeds and not much else, so they take most of the crop pool here.

theBottoms._biasNote: Standing water is a bird map, but the first cut of this bias made it a SOFT one and tests/run.test.ts said so: the Hand idle-buy bot cleared 6 of 24 standing still against a cap of 5. duckFlight was at 2.1 and it is `laneFly` -- it crosses the arena and never engages, so against a player who does not move it is a conveyor belt of free xp that cannot hit back. Cut to 1.3, and what it paid for went to the things that punish standing still: the feral dog flanks, the bloated farmhand gasses the ground you are on.

hazards._note: Sucking mud. Big, slow, long-lived and it does almost no damage -- the cost is that you are still standing in it when the next flight comes through. Density is life / everySeconds, which is the measurement session 16 got wrong.
hazards._playerDpsNote: 2 and not 0. At 0 the mud was free to stand in, which on a map whose signature enemy does not engage made the whole level cost a stationary player nothing at all. It is still the gentlest hazard in the game -- the Burn does 6 -- but it is no longer scenery.

place._note: The Bottoms as a place: the creek bottom below the farm, where the low ground never drained and the spray ran off into it. Standing water on every side, reeds and cattails at every edge, a rotten boardwalk out of the north gate, drowned snags, a wagon left to sink and an old fence line walking into the creek.

theVault.name: The Vault
theVault._dressingNote: No farm here. The default dressing is a barnyard -- ploughs, grave markers, scarecrows, fence rails -- and the first preview shot of this floor had all of it standing on concrete. Storage tanks and a service lift are what belongs on a bunker level; the blast door is deliberately NOT in this list because it is the level exit and a fixture the level system places, not something to scatter eleven of round the edges. Decals keep scorch and ash and drop mud and tyre ruts, which are outdoor marks.
theVault._boundaryNote: A room, not a field. `band` is what the wall occupies and `inset` is what the PLAYER is held off by -- equal here, so you stop at the wall's inner face rather than standing on it. Enemies are deliberately not inset: they spawn outside the arena and walk in, which is exactly what they already did through the farm's fence. Every surface map omits this block entirely and keeps inset 0, which is what makes their seeded replays byte-identical to before the wall existed.
theVault._exitNote: The way down. A DOOR IN THE WALL and not a portal, and the ordering matters: everything about this place -- poured concrete, stencils, a cage lift -- says people built it with the engineering they had, and a portal on level two throws that away for a magic door. The lift earns the portal by going deep enough that engineering stops explaining what is down there. Placed on the wall band, which is the second reason that band exists: a door in the middle of an open field is a prop.
theVault._overheadNote: A ceiling, so the room has a top. Strip lights and service runs rather than stalactites -- same layer, opposite vocabulary, which is the whole monotony break. `striplightDead` hangs at an angle off its cable and is the one that does the work: a room where SOME of the lights have failed reads as a place something happened to. It fades near the player like every overhead layer does, because a bullet-heaven player has to see what is about to hit them.

breakables._webNote: The webbed drum is a SKIN of the drum, not a class of its own -- the rule breakables.json states twice: hp, radius and drop table are what a class IS, and two skins of the same object must never pay differently. It appears only underground, which is the whole reason a map may replace a skin list: a web on a barn drum in an open field would be a lie about how long that field has been standing.

theVault._biasNote: The base roster. Zeroing the farm animals alone would leave six enemies across twenty-five waves with holes at 2, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16 and 19 -- which is the whole reason the base cast was generated. A cursed pony three floors under a missile silo is the sort of thing that makes a place read as randomly generated rather than built.

theLift.name: Sub-Level 2 — Lift Head
theLift._note: The second base level, and the proof that descending works: it shares theVault's arena EXACTLY, because `World.descendTo` refuses a map that would change it. The spatial grid, the camera and every canvas the renderer bakes are sized from the arena once, at construction, so levels of one facility share a footprint and a descent costs a re-bake instead of a rewrite. Rooms in one building; it costs the design nothing.
theLift._biasNote: Deeper, so the roster hardens: the chaff thins, the containment crews get commoner and the breacher only exists down here. Same principle as the wave curve, one floor at a time.

_fogNote: Ground fog is per-map and OFF by default -- a map that says nothing gets none. It is drawn above the ground and decals and below every sprite, so it lies on the floor rather than over the fight: two hundred enemies and their bullets are read against this ground, and ART_STYLE is explicit that the floor should be boring for exactly that reason. Fog is how a floor gets atmosphere WITHOUT getting contrast -- it lowers the ground's local contrast while adding depth, where a busier tile would raise it and start competing with the things the player has to read. `alpha` is the ceiling on the whole layer and is the number to turn down first if anything ever gets hard to see. Two banks drift at different speeds so the parallax reads as depth instead of as a moving texture.
_overheadNote: The overhead layer: art that hangs from a ceiling and draws OVER everything, including the player. Absent means a map has none, which every surface map is. It is the thing that makes a space read as enclosed rather than as a dark field -- a top-down game has no other way to say 'there is something above you', because every other sprite y-sorts against the ground. IT FADES WHEN THE PLAYER IS UNDER IT, to `minAlpha` within `fadeRadius`. Without that, a stalactite that covers the player is not atmosphere, it is an occluder in a game where you must see what is about to hit you -- and in a bullet-heaven the answer is never 'the player should move'. `minAlpha` is the number to raise if anything is ever lost under it. Placement is RENDER-SIDE and seeded off its own stream, the same rule as the scenery band and the decals: nothing decorative may move a tile, a decal or a spawn.
_dressingNote: Scenery and decals used to be TWO HARDCODED FARM LISTS inside the renderer, which is how the first bunker preview came out with pumpkins, a tree and farm rocks lying on a concrete floor. Fog, overhead art, breakable skins and the ground were already per-map; the dressing was the one layer that was not, so every new biome inherited a barnyard. It is data now. `defaultDressing` is what a map gets when it says nothing -- the farm set, so the five surface maps are unchanged to the pixel -- and a map's own `dressing` block REPLACES it wholesale rather than merging, because a bunker wants none of the farm and a merge would have meant listing ten exclusions to drop ten props. An empty array is a legal answer and means bare ground.
_twoMoreNote: `ranch.gateClosed` and `ranch.coopBroken` joined the list on 2026-09-04, both from the ledger's open queue and both by the rule above rather than around it. The closed gate is a second SKIN of a fixture the list already carries -- the same argument that put a galvanised trough beside a wooden one in breakables.json -- and a run of fence reading closed in one place and open in another is worth a line. The wrecked coop is the one that needed a tool fixed first: it came back on an opaque white card with a black rule drawn down two sides, and `npm run decard` matched only the CORNER colour, so it cut the white, left the rule, and reported a content box exactly the size of the canvas. decard now floods every colour the border ring is substantially made of, and the coop cuts to 76x87 -- a fixture, three-quarter view, the size of the hay wagon. No generation.
_generatedDressingNote: The seven `ranch.*` entries were packed in the atlas and drawn by NOTHING until the 2026-09-03 inventory audit -- generated for the title screen, and nobody ever asked whether they also belonged on the field. They do. Measured rather than judged: hayWagon is 87x81 of content and tractorRed 85x87, against prop.scarecrow 69x88 and prop.plough 60x47, in the same three-quarter view, and the farm they were drawn for is the farm this is. Every one is a FIXTURE, which is the rule this list obeys and the reason two of their sheet-mates are not here: `ranch.waterTrough` and `ranch.roundBaleRotted` are container-shaped and went into breakables.json as variants instead. An unbreakable trough standing beside a breakable one is the one thing no amount of feedback recovers from. v2 took `ranch.tractorRed` back OFF the field (critic round 2): the final boss is a rusted tractor, and a tractor parked in the field read as the boss, or the boss as furniture.
_fenceRailNote: `ranch.fenceRail` joined on the scene-pass audit, by the same rule as `_generatedDressingNote` above: a fixture generated for the title screen and never asked whether it also belonged on the field. It is a standalone post-and-rail section, `prop.fenceRail`'s sheet-mate rather than a duplicate of `ranch.fenceRun`/`fenceBroken`/`fenceCornerPost` -- those are a run, a break and a corner; this is the plain span between them. No generation.
